title: Drennon Springs Salt Works
summary: In Henry County, Jacob Drennon and Matthew Bracken claimed the big salt lick at Drennon Springs in 1773, and salt boiling works rose there in 1785.
bodyMarkdown:
Drennon Springs is a group of salt and mineral springs in Henry County. Over two centuries the springs drew animals, Native hunters, surveyors, salt makers and, later, summer visitors to a resort. Archaeologists working there in the 1990s documented one of the few early Kentucky salt works ever studied.

## A great lick

The Kentucky Historical Society's [Drennon Springs marker](https://history.ky.gov/markers/drennon-springs) says Native people found and used the springs for their medicinal properties. It records that Jacob Drennon and Matthew Bracken claimed the springs on July 26, 1773. Drennon was one of several men who surveyed this part of Henry County that year, and the springs still carry his name.

The McAfee surveying party passed the springs the same summer. According to [ExploreKYHistory](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/987), they followed Eagle Creek from the Kentucky River to Drennon Springs. They judged the land along the way poor for settlement because it lacked springs.

In 1775 the English traveler Nicholas Cresswell called Drennon's "the largest lick I ever saw." The [Kentucky Archaeological Survey's site page](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Drennon-Springs.aspx) quotes his account of about 50 acres trodden bare by buffalo. He also wrote that some springs were so briny that "the sun forms the salt round the edge."

## Clark's patent and the salt works

On April 1, 1785, Virginia governor Patrick Henry issued [George Rogers Clark](/stories/george-rogers-clark/) a patent for 400 acres that included the springs, according to the KHS marker. Salt making there began in the winter of 1785, according to the archaeology page.

Making salt from spring water took long periods of boiling and cooling to remove impurities and form crystals. A large works could employ more than 100 people to build furnaces, cut fuel wood, haul kettles and keep fires going. Many of these workers were enslaved, either by the springs' owner or by neighboring farmers who rented them out.

## What archaeologists found

In the 1990s, before a bridge was replaced, archaeologists from the Kentucky Transportation Cabinet and Wilbur Smith Associates excavated the works. The site is recorded as Omer Adams, after the landowner at the time. The team examined ten stone-lined furnace trenches, 13 to 67 feet long. Each had a firing chamber about five feet wide and a stone chimney on its east end, and the walls were burned red.

Two broken kettles came from the longest furnace. One had been built into the stone lining and the other lay in its firing chamber. They are the most complete salt kettles yet recovered from a Kentucky archaeological site.

## Kentucky today

The Kentucky Archaeological Survey does not publish the location of the salt-works site. KHS marker 122 also recalls the later Drennon Springs Hotel and the Western Military Academy, opened there in 1851. Other Kentucky salt works are described in [Bullitt's Lick](/stories/bullitts-lick-kentuckys-first-industry/) and [Mann's Lick](/stories/manns-lick-louisvilles-salt-town/).
